title: Analytical Nuclear Gradients and Hessians on Quantum Hardware via Orbital-Optimized VQE with Error Mitigation
authors: Renato Olarte Hernandez, Karl Michael Ziems, Erik Kjellgren, Jacob Kongsted, Sonia Coriani, Stephan P. A. Sauer
abstract: Nuclear gradients and Hessians are fundamental quantities in computational chemistry, essential for a wide range of applications including geometry optimization, vibrational spectroscopy, and molecular property calculations. In this work, we present their analytical implementation on quantum hardware. The methodology is formulated within an active-space framework combining orbital optimization and linear-response theory.   On the quantum-computing side, the approach employs the tiled unitary product state (tUPS) ansatz to directly evaluate the tensor elements required for solving the response equations. Moreover, the expectation values are corrected using an adapted confusion-matrix error-mitigation scheme in combination with post-selection criteria. The resulting workflow is assessed on molecular hydrogen and on water through the calculation of potential energy surfaces, nuclear gradients, Hessians, and vibrational frequencies, enabling the evaluation of both its capabilities and current limitations.   The results demonstrate good performance for the hydrogen molecule, whereas the water molecule provides a more demanding test of quantum-hardware resources and highlights the trade-offs associated with error-mitigation strategies. The quantified analysis of the results identify the main sources of errors, suggesting improvement directions for more accurate quantum computer applications.
summary: This paper presents a method to calculate fundamental chemical properties—nuclear gradients and Hessians—on quantum computers using an orbital-optimized VQE approach. By combining linear response theory with error mitigation techniques, the authors test their workflow on $	ext{H}_2$ and $	ext{H}_2	ext{O}$. The results validate the technique for small molecules while clearly mapping out current hardware limitations.
main_problem: The core problem is implementing the analytical calculation of nuclear gradients (first derivatives) and Hessians (second derivatives) for molecular energy with respect to nuclear coordinates directly on quantum hardware.
main_result: The methodology demonstrates good performance when tested on the hydrogen molecule ($	ext{H}_2$), although the water molecule ($	ext{H}_2	ext{O}$) reveals significant trade-offs related to current error mitigation strategies.
method: It combines an active-space framework with orbital optimization (oo-VQE) and utilizes a tiled unitary product state (tUPS) ansatz. Error mitigation is achieved using an adapted confusion-matrix scheme.
model_or_system: The calculations are performed for molecular systems, specifically testing on $	ext{H}_2$ and $	ext{H}_2	ext{O}$. The underlying theory uses the electronic Hamiltonian in second quantization within a linear-response framework.
key_observables: Potential energy surfaces, nuclear gradients ($\mathbf{E}^{(1)}$), Hessians ($\mathbf{E}^{(2)}$), and vibrational frequencies.
important_parameters: The complexity scales with the size of the molecule (e.g., $	ext{H}_2	ext{O}$ is more demanding than $	ext{H}_2$).
main_assumptions: The approach operates in a Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum (NISQ) context, necessitating quantum error mitigation techniques rather than full error correction.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the structure of the tiled-UPS ansatz used for the calculation.
paper_structure: The paper follows a standard scientific structure: Theory development $ightarrow$ Computational Methods detailing the oo-VQE and linear response implementation $ightarrow$ Results assessing performance on $	ext{H}_2$ and $	ext{H}_2	ext{O}$ $ightarrow$ Conclusion outlining error sources and future directions.
why_interesting: This work bridges advanced quantum chemistry (calculating derivatives for spectroscopy/optimization) with near-term quantum hardware limitations, providing a crucial benchmark for quantum simulation algorithms in molecular physics.
